questions.html: Which of the following is TRUE about Local $\text{DNS}$ name servers?

options.html: Cache resource records and never discard them.
Must be configured with a list of root name servers.
Never perform recursive queries on behalf of clients.
Always contacts the root name servers as part of every lookup.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 17)

The correct answer is:

"Must be configured with a list of root name servers."

Explanation of Each Option:

  1. Cache resource records and never discard them:
    This is false because local DNS servers cache resource records for a time defined by their Time-To-Live (TTL) value. Once the TTL expires, the records are discarded.The TTL field causes DNS servers to delete entries after some time, so that if the host moves and the underlying address changes, the server will eventually get the correct address.

  2. Must be configured with a list of root name servers:
    This is true because local DNS servers need to know how to contact root name servers to resolve domain names they cannot resolve locally. The list of root name servers (the root hints file) is a key configuration for a local DNS server.

  3. Never perform recursive queries on behalf of clients:
    This is false because local DNS servers often perform recursive queries to resolve domain names on behalf of their clients. Recursive queries involve the server contacting other DNS servers to fully resolve the requested name.

  4. Always contacts the root name servers as part of every lookup:
    This is false because a local DNS server will first check its cache for a record. If the desired record is found in the cache, it avoids contacting the root name servers.

Final Answer:

Must be configured with a list of root name servers.

Source solution 2 (score: 7)

The correct answer is Must be configured with a list of root name servers.

Local DNS name servers are responsible for resolving domain names to IP addresses for devices on their local network. They do this by caching resource records, which are small pieces of data that contain the IP address of a domain name. However, local DNS servers do not have all the resource records for all domain names in the world. Therefore, they must be configured with a list of root name servers, which are the top-level servers in the DNS hierarchy. When a local DNS server does not have the resource record for a domain name, it will forward the query to one of the root name servers. The root name server will then tell the local DNS server which TLD (top-level domain) name server to query next, and the process will continue until the local DNS server finally gets the resource record it needs.

Consider the following DNS Hierarchy.

Which of the following patterns represent a recursive query?

options.html: $\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{H}, \mathrm{I}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{G}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{C}$
$\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{H}, \mathrm{I}, \mathrm{G}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{G}, \mathrm{I}, \mathrm{H}, \mathrm{A}$
$\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{H}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{I}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{G}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{A}$
$\mathrm{I}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{G}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{H}, \mathrm{A}, \mathrm{H}$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

Please watch this video to understand the difference between Recursive and Iterative queries – DNS Video Link.

Option A is neither a Recursive nor Iterative query. It says $\mathrm{H} \rightarrow \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{H} \rightarrow \mathrm{I} \rightarrow \mathrm{A} \ldots$ Why would $\mathrm{I}$ reply to $\mathrm{A}$ even though $\mathrm{H}$ has just asked. Infact $\mathrm{I}$ does not even have address of $\mathrm{A}$.

Option B is a recursive query.

Option C is an iterative query.

Source solution 2 (score: 3)

ANSWER=B

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

We could check for sequence if in between breaks that won’t be our Answer.

Source solution 4 (score: 0)

Correct Answer: B

A, H, I, G, C, G, I, H, A

Explanation:

This question asks for the pattern of a Recursive Query.

  • Recursive Query: The burden of resolution is placed on the contacted server. The client (A) asks its server (H), "Go fetch the IP for C." H asks the next level (I), I asks the next (G), and G asks the target (C). The answer then bubbles back up the chain: C $\rightarrow$ G $\rightarrow$ I $\rightarrow$ H $\rightarrow$ A.

  • Iterative Query: The client does the work. The client asks the Root, gets a referral, then asks the TLD, gets a referral, etc. This would look like a "star" pattern (e.g., A $\rightarrow$ H, H $\rightarrow$ A, A $\rightarrow$ I, I $\rightarrow$ A...). This matches Option C.

Tracing Option B:

  1. A $\rightarrow$ H: yahoo.com server asks com server.

  2. H $\rightarrow$ I: com server asks Root server.

  3. I $\rightarrow$ G: Root server asks org server.

  4. G $\rightarrow$ C: org server asks pbs.org server.

  5. C $\rightarrow$ G $\rightarrow$ I $\rightarrow$ H $\rightarrow$ A: The answer travels back down the exact same path to the requester.

questions.html:
$$\text{"HTTP IS STATELESS."}$$
What do we mean when we say "HTTP is stateless"? In answering this question assume that cookies are not used. Select all the answers that apply.

options.html: An HTTP client does not remember anything about what happened during earlier steps in interacting with any HTTP server.
An HTTP client does not remember the identities of the servers with which it has interacted.
The HTTP protocol is not licensed in any country.
An HTTP server does not remember anything about what happened during earlier steps in interacting with this HTTP client.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 27)

I think somebody chose very unfortunate name for STATELESS concept and that's why the whole misunderstanding is caused. It's not about storing any kind of resources, but rather about the relationship between the client and the server.

Client: I'm keeping all the resources on my side and send you the "list" of all the important items which need to processed. Do your job.

Server: All right.. let me take the responsibility on filtering what's important to give you the proper response.

Which means that the server is the "slave" of the client and has to forget about his "master" after each request. Actually, STATELESS refers only to the state of the server.

For more you refer this link

https://www.ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/rest_arch_style.htm#sec_5_1_3

Source solution 2 (score: 9)

From Kurose,

It is important to note that the server sends requested files to clients without storing any state information about the client. If a particular client asks for the same object twice in a period of a few seconds, the server does not respond by saying that it just served the object to the client; instead, the server resends the object, as it has com- pletely forgotten what it did earlier. Because an HTTP server maintains no information about the clients, HTTP is said to be a stateless protocol

Source solution 3 (score: 3)

A protocol is called stateless if

    1) The server does not retain information (state) about the client between different requests.

    2) Every request from the client contains all the information the server needs to fulfill it.In HTTP requests, the server doesn't need to memorize about the client and can treat every request as a new interaction.

 

 (Unless session cookies is being stored, in which case upon every request the user will have to send the session cookie as well in the HTTP request, and the server can recognize the user by maintaining a database for it. But still the server is not necessarily remembering the connection, it is just storing a value for recognizing the session. The cookie can be reused by some other client machine and still the same state will be served pointing out that the session data is being stored and not necessarily the client data.)

So the correct answer is D

Source solution 4 (score: 0)

Correct Answer: D

"An HTTP server does not remember anything about what happened during earlier steps in interacting with this HTTP client."

Explanation:

  • Definition of Stateless: In the context of the HTTP protocol, "stateless" refers to the server-side behavior. It means the server treats every single HTTP request as a completely new, isolated event. It retains no information (state) about previous requests from the same client.

  • Why A is False: While the protocol is stateless, the Client (e.g., a web browser) often does remember things. It caches pages, remembers history, and stores cookies (even though the question says "assume cookies are not used," the definition of statelessness primarily constrains the server, not the client's ability to remember locally).

  • Context: This design simplifies the server design and allows it to handle thousands of simultaneous TCP connections without the overhead of maintaining session data for every single one.

options.html: A user requests a Web page that consists of some text and three images. For this page the client will send one request message and receive four response messages.
Two distinct Web pages (for example, $\textsf{www.duke.edu/research.html}$ and $\textsf{www.duke.edu/students.html})$ can be sent over the same persistent connection.
With non-persistent connections between browser and origin server, it is possible for a single TCP segment to carry two distinct HTTP request messages.
All of these are false.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 10)

This question is taken from Kurose and Ross Edition $6$ Exercise $2$ Question $\text{P1 (Page No 171)}$

  1. A user requests a Web page that consists of some text and three images. For this page the client will send one request message and receive four response messages. False. Send 4 receive 4.
  2. Two distinct Web pages (for example, $\textsf{www.duke.edu/research.html}$ and $\textsf{www.duke.edu/students.html})$ can be sent over the same persistent connection. True. Persistent HTTP leaves connection open.
  3. With non-persistent connections between browser and origin server, it is possible for a single TCP segment to carry two distinct HTTP request messages. False. Each TCP segment can only carry one request.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

ANSWER = B

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

Correct Answer: B

"Two distinct Web pages (for example, www.duke.edu/research.html and www.duke.edu/students.html) can be sent over the same persistent connection."

Explanation:

  • Why B is True: HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default. This means that a single TCP connection is kept open after a request is served, allowing the client to send subsequent requests (like a second HTML page or images located on the same server) over that same existing connection. Since both URLs in the example belong to the same host (www.duke.edu), the browser can reuse the connection.

  • Why A is False: HTTP works on a request-response basis. If a user requests a page with text and three images, the client must send a request for the HTML, receive it, parse it, and then send three separate requests for the three images. It does not send 1 request and get 4 discrete response messages automatically without asking for the images.

  • Why C is False: With non-persistent connections, the TCP connection is closed after the server sends the requested object. You cannot send a second request on the same connection, let alone pack two distinct requests into a single TCP segment.

questions.html:
Suppose within your Web browser you click on a link to obtain a web page. The IP address for the associated URL is not cached in your local host, so a DNS look-up is necessary to obtain the IP address. Suppose that $n$ DNS servers are visited before your host receives the IP address from DNS; the successive visits incur an $\mathrm{RTT}$ of $\mathrm{RTT}_1$, $\ldots, \mathrm{RTT}_{n}$. Further suppose that the web page associated with the link contains exactly one object, consisting of a small amount of a small amount of HTML text. Let $\text{RTT}$ denote the $\text{RTT}$ between the local host and the server containing the object. Assuming zero transmission time of the object, how much time elapses from when the client clicks on the link until the client receives the object?

In all options $\mathrm{X}=\text{RTT}_1+\text{RTT}_2+\ldots +\text{RTT}_n$.

options.html: $\text{RTT}_0+\mathrm{X}$
$2 \text{RTT}_0+\mathrm{X}$
$\mathrm{X}$
$\mathrm{X} / 2$

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 16)

The total amount of time to get the IP address is
$$
\text{RTT}_1+\text{RTT}_2+\ldots +\text{RTT}_n .
$$
Once the IP address is known, $\text{RTT}_0$ elapses to set up the TCP connection and another $\text{RTT}_0$ elapses to request and receive the small object. The total response time is
$$
2 \text{RTT}_0+\text{RTT}_1+\text{RTT}_2+\ldots +\text{RTT}_n .
$$

In a simple language we can understand it like it has been given in the question that before receving IP it has already done n RTTs while searching IP

Then after that we got that particular IP that we were searching

Now will we will search that webpage associated with that IP which will take 2RTT = 1 RTT(request & response)+1 RTT (small object)

Thus suming up all RTTs = 2RTT+ RTT1, RTT2....RTTn

questions.html: A user in Chicago, connected to the internet via a $100 \mathrm{~Mb} / \mathrm{s} \;(\text{b = bits})$ connection retrieves a $250 \;\text{KB (B = bytes)}$ web page from a server in London, where the page references three images of $500 \mathrm{~KB}$ each. Assume that the one-way propagation delay is $75 \mathrm{~ms}$ and that the user's access link is the bandwidth bottleneck for this connection. Approximately how long does it take for the page (including images) to appear on the user's screen, assuming non-persistent HTTP using a single connection at a time ( you should ignore queueing delay and transmission delays at other links in the network)?

options.html: $1.34 \;\text{seconds}$
$590 \mathrm{~ms}$
$320 \mathrm{~ms}$
$2.31 \;\text{seconds}$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 24)

With non-persistent HTTP, there is one TCP connection for the page and one for each one of the images. Each connection incurs a delay of $2^ \ast  \text{RTT}$ plus transmission time. Hence the total time until the page $+$ images shows up on the user's screen is calculated as follows:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text{RTT}=2  \ast  75 \mathrm{~ms}=150 \mathrm{~ms} \\
& \text { Transmission Time }=(\text { Amount of data }) /(\text { data rate })= \\
& ((250 \text { Kbytes }  \ast  8 \text { bits/byte })+(3  \ast  500 \text { Kbytes }  \ast  8 \text { bits/byte })) /(100 \times 10 \mathrm{Mbits} / \mathrm{sec})= \\
& (2 \mathrm{~Mbits}+3  \ast  4 \mathrm{~Mbits}) /(100 \mathrm{~Mbits} / \mathrm{s}) \\
& (\# \text{RTT})^ \ast (\text{RTT})+(\text { Transmission Time }) \\
& 2  \ast (3+1)  \ast  150 \mathrm{~ms}+(14 \mathrm{~Mb}) /(100 \mathrm{~Mb} / \mathrm{s})= \\
& 8  \ast  150 \mathrm{~ms}+\left(14  \ast  10^6 \mathrm{~bits}\right) / 100  \ast  10^6 \mathrm{~b} / \mathrm{sec}= \\
& 1200 \mathrm{~ms}+0.14 \mathrm{~sec}= \\
& 1200 \mathrm{~ms}+140 \mathrm{~ms}=1.34 \text { seconds }. \\
&
\end{aligned}
$$

Source solution 5 (score: 2)

Here are the step-by-step solutions for the two problems presented in your images.

Problem 1: Web Page Retrieval Time

Correct Answer: A (1.34 seconds)

1. Understand the Setup

  • Bandwidth ($R$): $100\text{ Mbps} = 100 \times 10^6\text{ bits/sec}$.

  • Propagation Delay ($D_{prop}$): $75\text{ ms} = 0.075\text{ sec}$ (One-way).

  • Round Trip Time (RTT): $2 \times 75\text{ ms} = 150\text{ ms} = 0.15\text{ sec}$.

  • Objects:

    • 1 HTML file: $250\text{ KB}$.

    • 3 Image files: $500\text{ KB}$ each.

  • Connection Type: Non-persistent HTTP, single connection at a time (Serial).

2. Calculate Transmission Delays ($D_{trans} = L / R$)

First, convert file sizes to bits ($1\text{ KB} = 1024 \times 8\text{ bits} = 8192\text{ bits}$).

  • HTML File ($250\text{ KB}$):

     

    $$L_{html} = 250 \times 8192 = 2,048,000\text{ bits}$$

    $$D_{trans(html)} = \frac{2,048,000}{100,000,000} \approx 0.0205\text{ sec}$$

  • One Image ($500\text{ KB}$):

     

    $$L_{img} = 500 \times 8192 = 4,096,000\text{ bits}$$

    $$D_{trans(img)} = \frac{4,096,000}{100,000,000} \approx 0.0410\text{ sec}$$

  • Total Transmission Time (1 HTML + 3 Images):

     

    $$0.0205 + 3(0.0410) = 0.0205 + 0.123 = \mathbf{0.1435\text{ sec}}$$

3. Calculate Delay from Handshakes and Requests (RTTs)

With Non-persistent HTTP, every object requires a new TCP connection.

  • Per Object Cost: 1 RTT for TCP Handshake + 1 RTT for HTTP Request/Response = 2 RTTs per object.

  • Total Objects: 4 (1 HTML + 3 Images).

  • Total RTTs: $4 \text{ objects} \times 2 \text{ RTTs/object} = 8 \text{ RTTs}$.

  • Total Propagation Time:

     

    $$8 \times 0.15\text{ sec} = \mathbf{1.20\text{ sec}}$$

4. Final Calculation

 

$$\text{Total Time} = \text{Total Propagation} + \text{Total Transmission}$$

$$\text{Total Time} = 1.20\text{ s} + 0.1435\text{ s} = 1.3435\text{ s}$$

 

Rounding to two decimal places gives 1.34 seconds.

questions.html: Suppose you have a client C, a local name server L, and authoritative name servers A_root, A_com, and A_foo.com, where A_x is the name server that knows about the name zone x (and A_root is a root name server). C wants to lookup the address for www.foo.com. Assuming that all name servers initially have nothing in their cache, which of the following order of events is correct?

options.html: C asks L, L asks A_root, A_root tells L to ask A_com, L asks A_com, A_com tells L to ask A_foo.com, L asks A_foo.com, A_foo.com answers to L, L answers to C.
C asks A_root, A_root tells C to ask A_com, C asks A_com, A_com tells C to ask A_foo.com, C asks A_foo.com, A_foo.com answers to C, C tells L the address.
C asks L, L asks A_root, A_root asks A_com, A_com asks A_foo.com, A_foo.com answers to C.
C asks L, L asks A_foo.com, A_foo.com answers to L, L answers to C.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

The correct sequence of events for a DNS lookup in this scenario is:

C asks L, L asks A_root, A_root tells L to ask A_com, L asks A_com, A_com tells L to ask A_foo.com, L asks A_foo.com, A_foo.com answers to L, L answers to C.

Explanation:

  1. C asks L: The client (C) queries the local DNS resolver (L) for the IP address of www.foo.com.

  2. L asks A_root: The local DNS resolver does not have the answer in its cache, so it queries the root name server (A_root).

  3. A_root tells L to ask A_com: The root name server responds with a referral, directing L to the .com authoritative name server (A_com).

  4. L asks A_com: The local resolver queries A_com for www.foo.com.

  5. A_com tells L to ask A_foo.com: The .com name server responds with a referral to the authoritative name server for the foo.com zone (A_foo.com).

  6. L asks A_foo.com: The local resolver queries A_foo.com for www.foo.com.

  7. A_foo.com answers to L: The authoritative name server responds with the IP address of www.foo.com.

  8. L answers to C: The local resolver sends the IP address back to the client.

This process is consistent with the iterative DNS resolution process where the local DNS resolver (L) performs the querying on behalf of the client.

Case $3: \quad 10+100+60+80+60+100+10=420 \mathrm{~ms}.$

Source solution 4 (score: 2)

## Case 1: DNS Query is Cached (Correct Time: 20 ms)

In this scenario, the Local DNS server already has the IP address stored in its cache.

  • Process: The Requesting Host sends a query to the Local DNS Server, which immediately finds the answer and sends it back.

  • Calculation: The total time is one simple round trip between the host and the local server.

    • Time for query (Host → Local DNS): 10 ms

    • Time for reply (Local DNS → Host): 10 ms

    • Total Time = 10 ms + 10 ms = 20 ms

This confirms that statement A is correct.

## Case 2: DNS Query is Iterative (Correct Time: 340 ms)

In an iterative query, the Local DNS Server does all the work by asking each server in the hierarchy one by one.

  • Process:

    1. The Host sends the query to the Local DNS Server (10 ms).

    2. The Local Server queries the Root Server and gets a referral (Round Trip: 2 x 100 ms).

    3. The Local Server queries the TLD Server and gets a referral (Round Trip: 2 x 40 ms).

    4. The Local Server queries the Authoritative Server and gets the final answer (Round Trip: 2 x 20 ms).

    5. The Local Server sends the final answer back to the Host (10 ms).

  • Calculation:

    • Initial Query Trip (Host → Local): 10 ms

    • Round trip to Root: 200 ms

    • Round trip to TLD: 80 ms

    • Round trip to Authoritative: 40 ms

    • Final Reply Trip (Local → Host): 10 ms

    • Total Time = 10 + 200 + 80 + 40 + 10 = 340 ms

This confirms that statement B is correct.

## Case 3: DNS Query is Recursive (Correct Time: 420 ms)

In a purely recursive query (as interpreted for this problem), each server forwards the query to the next server down the line until the answer is found, which then travels back up the same chain.

  • Process: The query is passed down the hierarchy (Host → Local → Root → TLD → Authoritative), and the answer is passed back up the same path.

  • Calculation: We sum the one-way propagation delays for the entire path down and back up.

    • Forward Path (Query): 10ms (Host→Local) + 100ms (Local→Root) + 60ms (Root→TLD) + 40ms (TLD→Auth) = 210 ms

    • Return Path (Reply): 40ms (Auth→TLD) + 60ms (TLD→Root) + 100ms (Root→Local) + 10ms (Local→Host) = 210 ms

    • Total Time = 210 ms + 210 ms = 420 ms

This confirms that statement C is correct.

Source solution 5 (score: 0)

Based on the calculations below, statements A, B, and C are ALL Correct. 

Scenario Breakdown & Calculations:

  • Case 1: Query Cached in Local DNS

    • Path: Host ↔ Local DNS

    • Math: 2×(Host-Local Delay)=2×10 ms=20 ms.

    • Conclusion: Option A is TRUE.

  • Case 2: Iterative Query

    • Definition: The Local DNS server queries each server (Root, TLD, Authoritative) one by one on behalf of the host.

    • Steps:

      1. Host ↔ Local: 2×10=20 ms.

      2. Local ↔ Root: 2×100=200 ms.

      3. Local ↔ TLD: 2×40=80 ms.

      4. Local ↔ Authoritative: 2×20=40 ms.

    • Total: 20+200+80+40=340 ms.

    • Conclusion: Option B is TRUE. Option D (330 ms) is FALSE.

  • Case 3: Recursive Query

    • Definition: The query is passed from server to server (Host → Local → Root → TLD → Auth) and the answer bubbles back up the same chain.

    • One-Way Path: Host(10) + Root(100) + TLD(60) + Auth(40). (Note: We use the direct links between servers shown in the diagram for the recursive steps).

    • One-Way Sum: 10+100+60+40=210 ms.

    • Round Trip: 2×210=420 ms.

    • Conclusion: Option C is TRUE.

Summary of Valid Statements:

  • A. In Case 1 time is 20 ms

  • B. In Case 2 time is 340 ms

  • C. In Case 3 time is 420 ms
